description: AI Engineer, Technical Strategist and Kaggle Master.
summary:
Astale: Real-time fire command for space crews

Most tools for fire safety in space are libraries of data. Astale tells the crew what to do, right now.

In microgravity, flames are round and almost invisible, and smoke does not rise. The crew has seconds to act. NASA’s own research shows that under stress, even trained memory fails. Apollo 1 showed how fast a cabin fire can turn deadly.

When a fire starts, Astale sounds the alarm and gives each person their own order: the commander, the crew and ground control. For example: “Put on your oxygen mask now.” “Cut the ventilation.” “Fire the extinguisher.” Each order comes with a timer, a ✓ DONE button and a one-line reason. When a step is done, the next one appears. The plan ends with a visual check and a damage report.

The orders are calculated, not generic. They change with the vehicle (ISS, Orion, a Moon base or a Mars base), the material on fire, gravity, oxygen level, cabin volume and radio delay. Every order cites its NASA source.

Behind the orders:

NASA PSI experiments: BASS-II, Saffire, FLEX.
Our own Super-Intelligence, trained on 257 real ISS flames (R² 0.70, AUC 0.89).
Fire Twin, a digital twin that shows how long the crew has before the air becomes dangerous.

Estimated impact: 20% less risk and 20% less damage.

Team Astale Zarqalis · astale.com
details:
PROJECT GITHUB

Flame in Freefall asks for a Super-Intelligence-powered dashboard that summarizes, organizes and interprets NASA’s PSI combustion experiments. Astale does the four things the challenge lists:
- Ranks the PSI combustion investigations by how relevant each one is to a given mission and material.
- Turns their raw test tables into model-ready data and trains our own Super-Intelligence on them (257 FLEX flames).
- Converts the results into design and safety guidance, which become the orders the crew follows.
- Shows how the same knowledge applies on Earth (could be used in airplanes, submarines, oil refineries,...).
The difference is that the output is not a chart. It is an action.



Astale started from the question: if a fire broke out on a spacecraft right now, would the crew know exactly what to do in the next thirty seconds? NASA’s own human-factors research says that under extreme stress people can panic and underperform and even well-trained memory fails. In microgravity the problem gets worse, because flames are round and almost invisible and smoke doesn’t rise. We didn’t want to build another library of combustion data. We wanted to build something a commander could actually use during an emergency.

So Astale works like a fire command system. You can simulate where the crew is (the ISS, Orion, a Moon base or a Mars base) and which area is burning, and the alarm goes off. Each person picks their role: commander, crew member or ground control. From there, each one sees only their own next order, written in plain words: “Put on your oxygen mask now”, “Cut the ventilation”, “Fire the CO₂ extinguisher”. Every order has a timer, a DONE button and one line explaining why. That line uses a number calculated for that exact scenario, such as how much oxygen will be left after the extinguisher is discharged compared with the limit NASA measured in BASS-II, or how long until the CO in that cabin becomes dangerous. Next to the orders there is a map of the vehicle, a thermal camera view, the CO level in each room and the radio delay to Earth, which on Mars can reach 22 minutes. That’s long enough that the crew has to decide alone. At the end, the crew has to confirm with their own eyes that the fire is out. If it isn’t, the plan adds steps. Afterwards they inspect the damage and get an incident report.

Most of what is behind those orders comes from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics database, mainly the BASS-II, Saffire and FLEX experiments, plus NASA technical reports. NASA's PSI experimentation does not cover all combinations of habitat/materials, so we also trained our own prediction model on 257 real flames burned on the ISS. It combines XGBoost, CatBoost, a random forest and a linear model, all written from scratch in JavaScript, and it trains directly in the browser. It predicts burning rate with an R² of 0.70 and whether a flame will go out by itself with an AUC of 0.89, both checked with cross-validation. The Fire Twin, a live animated simulation of the flame, the smoke and the crew, shows the same fire with and without a plan, so you can see how much time the plan buys.

We estimate it could reduce the risk of a fire getting out of control by around 20%, and the damage by a similar amount, for any crewed mission. That matters more the farther we go from Earth. The same idea also works down here: submarines, aircraft, offshore platforms, and any closed place where people can’t simply walk out.

What we think makes Astale different is the change of point of view. Most projects in this challenge look at NASA’s combustion data from the researcher’s side, as something to search, chart and compare. We looked at it from inside the cabin, from the person who has the fire in front of them. That’s why the data never appears on its own (until the very end in the report): it is turned into orders. Each person gets their own orders, because in a real emergency the commander, the crew and ground control don’t need the same information. The plan reacts to what the crew does and to what they see, so if they say the fire is still burning, the plan changes. Even the visuals follow that idea. We drew the flame the way it really looks in microgravity, a quiet blue sphere that is easy to miss, because a crew trained on flames as we know them on Earth might not recognise the danger. The thermal camera and the radio delay to Mars come from the same place: we kept asking what it would actually feel like to be in that cabin.

We were strict with ourselves about honesty. Every number is labelled as measured by NASA, taken from NASA literature, or our own assumption. When we have to estimate something NASA never tested, such as a fire in a lunar habitat atmosphere, we assume the more dangerous case and say which experiment is missing. We also cared about realism. The flame is drawn the way NASA filmed it in microgravity, and the crew wears normal clothes inside the cabin and puts on masks when the alarm sounds, not spacesuits.


A WORKED CASE:

Fire in a Moon base laboratory. A lunar habitat runs on an “exploration atmosphere”: 34% oxygen at reduced pressure, at one-sixth of Earth’s gravity. NASA has never burned a test in exactly these conditions, so Astale flags the case as an estimate and takes the more dangerous end. It classifies the incident as Class 3 · Critical.

Without a plan: a fire the size of NASA’s Saffire VI tests (1.5–3.2 kW) in a 30 m³ module pushes carbon monoxide past 425 ppm, NASA’s one-hour limit, in about 42 seconds.

With Astale, the commander’s first order is not “fight the fire”. It is “Put on your oxygen mask now, before anything else”, because the CO₂ extinguisher the crew is about to use will leave the module at the equivalent of 5% CO₂, which is hard to breathe without a mask.



The second order is to raise the alarm. At 34% oxygen, a flame that would barely survive on the ISS burns hard, so the next order is to use the extinguisher at once rather than wait for it to self-extinguish. Then: prepare to evacuate to the airlock, and watch for re-ignition, because in low gravity hot gas rises slowly and the flame can come back.

The full plan has 13 actions in 14 minutes, split between the commander, the crew and ground control (1.3 s radio delay). It ends with a visual check: if the crew reports “still burning”, Astale adds a second extinguisher step before allowing the damage inspection.

After the fire has been extinguished, there is a scientific incident report, focused on all stakeholders (crew, earth control,...).


EXTRA TECHNICAL INFO:

Behind every order there is a number, and behind every number there is a source. We started from the 24 combustion investigations in NASA’s PSI database and used their raw test tables. We fitted each model to real measurements and then checked it by leaving one test out at a time and predicting it from the rest. For example, our model of the oxygen level at which a flame goes out comes from BASS-II, and it predicts the tests it hasn’t seen to within about 1.4 percentage points of oxygen. Our model of how fast CO builds up in the cabin is calibrated against Saffire, the large fires NASA burned inside empty cargo vehicles. Our machine-learning model was validated with 5-fold cross-validation using a fixed random seed, so anyone can reproduce the result, and it warns the user when a question falls outside the data it was trained on. We kept a ledger of every value in the system, and each one carries a label: measured by NASA, taken from NASA’s technical literature (mostly reports from the NASA Technical Reports Server), or an assumption of our own. Our assumptions are listed in one place so they are easy to question. The CO limit we use, 425 ppm for one hour, is NASA’s own exposure limit for spacecraft. The extinguisher in our calculations has the same 2.7 kg CO₂ charge as the ones on the ISS. Where no experiment exists, we don’t hide the gap. We estimate within the range that physics allows, we take the more dangerous end, and we say which test would be needed to close it.

The site is built in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Canvas for the graphics, Web Audio for the siren and Web Speech for voice commands. It runs on Netlify Functions written in TypeScript, uses Node scripts to pull the NASA data, and uses ffmpeg to put the video together. We used Claude Code as a coding assistant to move faster. It runs in any browser with nothing to install, in English and Spanish, and we designed it first for a tablet.
